_comment: Surgery pathway for benign prostatic hyperplasia with urinary retention. Shared examination, history, approach and annexure skills are referenced, never redefined; disease-owned skills are reasoning, investigation and treatment only. History risk-factor and presentation skills live in the shared fragment and are merged into the pack by the lead.

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Prostatic enlargement is a disease of men over 50, rare below that age. A slow urinary story in a 68 year old carries a different weight from the same story at 30, where stricture or stone leads. Record residence and travel too: a man who holds urine for hours on buses without toilets arrives with a fuller bladder and a worse story.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: Years of weak stream ending in hours of inability

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: A typical presentation reads in years, then hours: weak stream and night frequency for three years, then no urine since last night with lower abdominal pain. That two-scale tempo alone names acute on chronic retention before anything is examined.

skill.hx.surg.urinary_symptoms.expect: Expect the full voiding set: hesitancy, a stream that falls without force, straining that worsens rather than improves flow, a bladder that never feels empty, and dribbling after. With it expect the storage set: night frequency first, then day frequency, urgency with urge leakage. Ask specifically about terminal red urine, burning with fever, and which new tablet preceded the stoppage.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Why it blocked now and what treatment is safe

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: The price late disease charges the whole body

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for a restless man pressing his lower abdomen in acute retention, or a cheerful one who does not know his bladder reaches near the navel. Note pallor of chronic disease, a dry coated tongue with drowsiness suggesting uraemia, and diabetic clues that also explain bladder numbness.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Expect a raised blood pressure in a man with back-pressure kidneys, and fever with a fast pulse when infected retention has supervened. Count the pulse and pressure yourself: an older man on new bladder medicines falls easily, and the first prescription must be judged against these numbers.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Ankle swelling that fades by morning in a retained man points to fluid retention from failing kidneys or to cardiac disease that also fills the bladder overnight. Press, time it, and pit it: non-pitting swelling is not this story.

chapters.title: Abdominal, genital and rectal examination
chapters.blurb: Dome above, kidneys behind, prostate below

skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.expect: Expect ballotable kidneys with tenderness at the renal angles in back-pressure disease, rather than the impalpable kidneys of health. A tender full kidney with a raised urea is obstruction speaking from above.

skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.expect: Expect a smooth symmetrical midline dome arising from behind the pubic bone, dull with a convex upper border: tense and tender in this acute presentation, soft and painless in the chronic cases you will also meet. Confirm it vanishes after catheterisation.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.expect: Expect normal anal tone and smooth rectal walls with no blood on the glove in uncomplicated enlargement; the finger then turns anterior to read the prostate separately. Any rectal mass, stricture discharge, or blood changes the whole investigation line.

skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.expect: Expect a symmetrically enlarged firm rubbery gland with a smooth surface, a preserved central groove, and freely mobile rectal lining, non-tender. A stony nodule, a lost groove, asymmetry, or tethered lining in this same examination is cancer until proven otherwise, even when the rest feels benign.

stations.title: Examine the abdomen and prostate
stations.task: This 68-year-old man has been unable to pass urine since last night. Examine his abdomen, loins and prostate and present your findings.
examinerQuestions: You found a dull midline dome you cannot get below. Why is that finding dull, and what single bedside check confirms what it is?
Your prostate feel is smooth and symmetrical with a preserved groove. What two finger findings would force you to suspect cancer instead?
His urea is raised with creatinine at the upper limit. What does that change in your plan tonight?

stations.title: Take a urinary history and grade the burden
stations.task: This 68-year-old man reports years of weak stream and night-time frequency. Take a focused history in six minutes and be ready to grade his symptom burden.
examinerQuestions: Score his burden from what you found, and state which answers carried the most weight.
Which medicine in his story most likely precipitated last night's retention, and by what mechanism?
Name two findings in the history that would make you refer him the same day.

skill.bph.basics.title: What benign prostatic hyperplasia is
skill.bph.basics.oneLine: Slow enlargement of the inner prostate squeezing the passage, in men over 50
skill.bph.basics.why: BPH is common, slow and benign, yet it produces the commonest surgical cause of retention in men. Holding its mechanism clearly, a static squeeze plus a muscular grip plus a tired bladder wall, lets every symptom and every treatment choice fall into place.

teach.heading: A disease of age and hormones
teach.body:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a non-cancerous overgrowth of gland and muscle around the urinary passage, almost never seen below 50 and troubling men most between 50 and 70. Growth is driven by years of male hormone action on the prostate, and the inner tissue presses the outer rim into a firm false capsule that the finger feels as smooth enlargement.

It is slow hyperplasia of the inner gland, not cancer, and it starts in the zone around the passage while cancer usually starts in the outer zone. That geography is why early enlargement obstructs first while early cancer spreads silently first.

teach.heading: Two grips on the passage
teach.body:
The enlarged gland narrows the passage mechanically, which is the static grip, and extra muscle tone in the gland and bladder neck grips it further, which is the dynamic grip. This dual grip is why one drug relaxes the muscle within weeks while another must shrink the gland over months.

Downstream the bladder wall thickens to push harder, then tires: the pouch behind the gland holds residual urine, the wall forms pockets, and in late disease pressure climbs back to the kidneys. Size alone misleads throughout, since a small hidden lobe can block badly while a large gland may barely trouble its owner.

teach.heading: Median lobe versus lateral lobes
points: A median lobe, felt poorly or not at all, gives mainly irritative symptoms: night frequency and urgency.
Lateral lobe enlargement gives mainly obstructive symptoms: hesitancy, slow stream and terminal dribbling.
Straining can press the median lobe onto the outlet and worsen the block, so a poor stream that straining fails to improve points to the prostate.

probes.q: At what age does BPH become common, and where in the gland does it start?
probes.a: Almost never below 50, usually presenting between 50 and 70; it starts in the inner tissue around the urinary passage, compressing the outer gland into a false capsule.

probes.q: Explain the static and dynamic components of obstruction in BPH.
probes.a: The static component is mechanical narrowing by the enlarged gland; the dynamic component is extra smooth muscle tone in the gland and bladder neck. Muscle relaxants ease the dynamic grip quickly, while shrinkers act on the static bulk over months.

probes.q: Why can a prostate that feels normal still cause severe obstruction?
probes.a: An enlarged median lobe cannot be felt per rectum but projects into the bladder outlet, giving mainly irritative symptoms; cystoscopy, not the finger, detects it.

pitfalls: Equating gland size with symptom severity when deciding treatment.
Calling every prostate symptom cancer, or every prostate swelling benign, without examining for nodules and the groove.
Forgetting the bladder wall story: thickening, residual urine and back pressure are the disease, not the grams.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.bph.retention.title: Urinary retention: recognising acute, chronic and acute on chronic
skill.bph.retention.oneLine: Painful sudden blockage over a silent chronic build-up, and why the painless one harms more
skill.bph.retention.why: Acute retention is the emergency the patient begs to be relieved of; chronic retention is the painless dome the patient cheerfully ignores while pressure climbs to the kidneys. Telling them apart at the bedside decides whether the next step is urgent relief, planned relief with protection of the kidneys, or both.

teach.heading: Acute retention
teach.body:
Acute retention is a sudden inability to pass urine with severe lower abdominal pain and a desperate urge to void. A pure first attack in a previously normal bladder is rare, seen after anaesthesia, injury or operation; in most men an unnoticed chronic build-up precedes it, so the event is really acute on chronic, often triggered by a cold remedy, alcohol, constipation, a loaded rectum, or enforced bed rest.

On examination the bladder forms a tense tender midline dome rising from behind the pubic bone, dull to percussion, and pressure on it sharpens the urge. The prostate cannot be judged while the bladder is full, so relief comes first and assessment after.

teach.heading: Chronic retention
teach.body:
Chronic retention is a gradual painless accumulation from never emptying fully, and the man may reach the clinic for dribbling, overflow leakage, night frequency or uraemic symptoms rather than for passing no urine. The dome may reach the navel yet stay soft and non-tender, and pressing it does not wake the urge, which is the bedside contrast with acute retention.

Infection turns chronic retention painful and febrile, which is then called acute on chronic. Never confuse retention with no urine formation: in retention the kidneys work and the bladder fills, while in anuria the bladder stays empty and collapsed.

teach.heading: Red flags that escalate the case
points: Any acute retention: an emergency needing same-day catheter relief.
Fever with a tender prostate or infected retained urine: retention with infection needs urgent drainage and assessment.
Vomiting, drowsiness, headache or ankle swelling with retention: possible uraemia from back pressure, so check kidney function and the upper tracts.
Visible blood, recurrent infection, stones, or a hard nodular gland: look beyond BPH to growth, stone or stricture.

probes.q: Contrast acute and chronic retention at the bedside.
probes.a: Acute retention is sudden and painful, with a tense tender suprapubic dome where pressure sharpens the urge; chronic retention is gradual and painless, the dome may reach the navel yet stays soft, and pressure does not wake the urge.

probes.q: A man passes small amounts frequently and wets himself at night, yet his bladder reaches near the navel. Explain.
probes.a: This is chronic retention with overflow leakage: the bladder never empties, so urine spills over continuously. It is easily mistaken for simple urge leakage, and the palpable dome is the clue.

probes.q: How do you separate retention from anuria at the bedside?
probes.a: In retention the kidneys form urine normally and the bladder is full and distended; in anuria the kidneys fail to excrete and the bladder is empty and collapsed. Percussion and catheterisation settle it.

pitfalls: Calling overflow leakage simple incontinence and missing the silent dome behind it.
Trying to judge prostate size while the bladder is still full, when the dome pushes everything backwards.
Reassuring a painless chronic retention as harmless because the patient looks cheerful.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The prostate and seminal vesicles: retention of urine

skill.bph.signs.title: Putting the retention picture together
skill.bph.signs.oneLine: Dome above, kidneys behind, prostate below: one obstruction read in three places
skill.bph.signs.why: The findings of prostatic obstruction are spread across three stations that students examine separately and forget to connect. A suprapubic dome means little until the kidneys and the prostate are read with it, and the trio together separates a simple enlarged gland from back-pressure disease.

teach.heading: The dome
teach.body:
A full bladder is the commonest midline mass below the navel: smooth, symmetrical, arising from behind the pubic bone so the finger cannot get below it, dull to percussion with the dullness convex upward. Tenderness marks the acute painful form; a soft painless dome marks the chronic form the patient may not know he carries.

Map it by palpating downward from resonant bowel, never upward from the bone, and confirm it disappears after catheterisation. Forgetting the bladder before any needle tap of the lower abdomen is the classic catastrophe this examination exists to prevent.

teach.heading: The kidneys and the general survey
teach.body:
Palpate both loins for enlargement and tenderness, since back pressure shows first as a tender full kidney and later as silent dilatation of the upper tracts. Read the general survey for the price of late disease: a dry coated tongue with drowsiness, pallor of chronic disease, puffy face or ankle swelling, and raised blood pressure in a man who never had hypertension.

Examine the penis, testes and perineum in the same sitting: a tight foreskin, meatal narrowing, urethral thickening or discharge, and perineal swelling or fistula each move the diagnosis away from the prostate alone.

teach.heading: The prostate feel
teach.body:
With the bladder empty, the benign gland feels symmetrically enlarged, firm and rubbery, smooth with small rounded bosses, the central groove preserved and the rectal lining moving freely over it. The finger may not reach the top of a large gland, and a lone median lobe may escape the finger entirely, so a normal feel never rules out obstruction.

A stony hard nodule, loss of the groove, asymmetry, or lining tethered to the gland points to cancer, even inside an otherwise benign-feeling gland. Tenderness with heat points to infection, where vigorous massage is forbidden because it can seed bacteria into the blood.

probes.q: What are the bedside marks of a distended bladder?
probes.a: A smooth symmetrical midline dome arising from behind the pubic bone so the finger cannot get below it, dull to percussion with the dullness convex upward, tender in acute retention and painless in chronic retention.

probes.q: What general and loin findings suggest back-pressure disease rather than simple enlargement?
probes.a: Tender or ballotable kidneys, a dry coated tongue with drowsiness, pallor, ankle swelling and newly raised blood pressure point to back pressure with uraemia rather than uncomplicated enlargement.

probes.q: How does the benign prostate feel, and what single finding most strongly points to cancer?
probes.a: The benign gland is symmetrically enlarged, firm and rubbery, smooth, with a preserved central groove and freely mobile rectal lining. A stony hard nodule with a lost groove and tethered lining points most strongly to cancer.

pitfalls: Palpating upward from the pubic bone and missing a dome that reaches the navel.
Declaring the prostate normal by finger when a median lobe is doing all the blocking.
Examining the prostate while the bladder is still full and misjudging its size.

sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: History and examination of the urinary tract

skill.bph.differential.title: What else blocks, irritates or bleeds in the older man
skill.bph.differential.oneLine: Cancer, stricture, nerve disease and bladder disease all wear the same urinary mask
skill.bph.differential.why: Most slow-stream older men do have prostatic enlargement, but the ones who do not carry cancer, stricture or nerve disease that punishes late diagnosis. The differential is not an academic list; it is the set of traps that turns a routine prostate clinic into a missed cancer or a needless operation.

rows: Carcinoma of the prostate
Short rapidly worsening course, weight loss, back pain, hard nodular gland with lost groove
Smooth symmetrical gland with preserved groove
Urethral stricture
Younger man, old discharge or instruments, stream that improves with straining
Stream that straining worsens, smooth prostatic enlargement
Bladder neck contracture
Previous prostate operation or instrumentation, poor stream persisting after surgery
No prior instrumentation, large smooth gland
Neurogenic bladder
Sugar disease, Parkinson disease, stroke, spinal disease, numb perineum
Normal nerves, palpable obstruction with intact sensation
Overactive bladder
Urgency and frequency with small voids and no residual urine
Large residual, weak stream, palpable dome
Urinary infection or prostatitis
Burning, fever, tender prostate, pus cells in urine
No burning, sterile urine, smooth non-tender gland
Bladder stone or tumour
Visible blood, sudden stoppage eased by posture change, weight loss
No blood, no stoppage, clear imaging

teach.heading: Cancer hiding inside BPH
teach.body:
Cancer and BPH share age, frequency, weak stream and retention, and cancer can grow inside an already enlarged gland. Suspect it when the course is short and rapidly worsening, when weight and appetite fall, when back pain or sciatica appears, or when the finger finds even one hard nodule or a lost groove.

A raised or rising marker after counselling, blood in the urine, or retention that keeps returning all demand exclusion of malignancy rather than another course of tablets. In India, tuberculosis of the urinary tract stays on the list when sterile pus persists in acid urine.

teach.heading: Do not forget the non-prostate causes
teach.body:
Sugar disease fills the bladder with sugar-driven urine and numbs its nerves; heart failure and evening water tablets fill it overnight; constipation and a loaded rectum press on the outlet. Medicines for cold, allergy, mood and gut spasm all tighten or weaken the system at once.

Night-time frequency deserves its own arithmetic: a bladder diary over three days separates true outlet obstruction from extra night-time urine production. Blaming the prostate for all lower urinary symptoms without testing urine, checking sugar and reviewing drugs is the commonest error in this clinic.

probes.q: Name four non-prostatic causes of lower urinary tract symptoms in an older man.
probes.a: Urethral stricture, neurogenic bladder from sugar disease or spinal disease, overactive bladder, urinary infection or prostatitis, and bladder stone or tumour.

probes.q: How do you separate a stricture from prostatic enlargement by history alone?
probes.a: A stricture follows old discharge, injury or instruments, affects younger men, and the stream improves with straining; prostatic obstruction affects older men and straining worsens the stream.

probes.q: When should cancer be suspected inside a benign-feeling prostate?
probes.a: With a short rapidly worsening course, weight loss, back pain or sciatica, a raised or rising marker, recurrent retention or visible blood, or even one hard nodule or lost groove on careful re-examination.

pitfalls: Stopping the differential at BPH because the age and stream fit.
Accepting visible blood as infection without excluding growth or stone.
Missing nerve disease because the prostate felt enlarged and nobody tested sensation.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.ix.bph.workup.title: Confirming obstruction, grading damage, excluding cancer
skill.ix.bph.workup.oneLine: Urine and kidneys first, the marker only after counselling, the stream as numbers
skill.ix.bph.workup.why: Investigations in prostatic disease answer three separate questions: is there infection or blood, have the kidneys suffered, and is this cancer. Tests sent in the wrong order, a marker drawn during retention or an operation booked without a residual volume, waste the very answers treatment depends on.

teach.heading: Every man gets these
teach.body:
Urine testing comes first: routine examination with microscopy and culture excludes infection, blood and sugar, and a properly collected mid-stream sample is the specimen that counts. Kidney function follows in every retained or obstructed man, since a raised urea with a climbing creatinine is the earliest warning of back pressure, and anaemia and sugar complete the fitness picture.

The prostate marker is measured only after counselling, because enlargement itself raises it mildly while a high or rising value demands cancer evaluation. Never draw it during infection or retention or soon after instrumentation, and remember that gland-shrinking drugs roughly halve it after months of use, so double the measured value when watching for cancer in treated men.

teach.heading: Measure the blockage
teach.body:
Post-void residual volume by bedside bladder scan tells how much the bladder keeps back after its best void, and uroflowmetry draws the stream as a flattened prolonged curve with a reduced peak. Together they turn a weak stream into numbers that can be followed through treatment.

Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder maps gland size, bladder wall thickening with pockets, stones and clots, and, crucially, whether the upper tracts are dilated. A three-day bladder diary separates outlet obstruction from extra night-time urine production when storage symptoms dominate.

teach.heading: Reserve these for questions
points: Pressure-flow studies when the picture is mixed: small voided volumes, good flow with symptoms, previous failed treatment, or extremes of age.
Cystoscopy to exclude a pocket, stone or growth, especially before an operation not done through the bladder.
Transrectal imaging and needle sampling when the marker is high or the gland feels hard and irregular.
Plain and contrast imaging of the urinary tract when stones, tuberculosis or upper tract disease is suspected.

probes.q: Which two bedside tests turn a weak stream into followable numbers?
probes.a: Post-void residual volume by bladder scan and uroflowmetry with its flattened prolonged curve and reduced peak flow.

probes.q: When should the prostate marker not be drawn, and why?
probes.a: Not during urinary infection, retention, or soon after instrumentation, because each raises it independently; and only after counselling, because even benign enlargement raises it mildly.

probes.q: A treated man on a gland-shrinking drug has a marker reading that looks reassuring. What is the catch?
probes.a: The drug roughly halves the marker after months of use, so double the measured value when watching for cancer, or a real rise will hide inside the normal range.

pitfalls: Drawing the marker during retention or infection and then chasing a meaningless rise.
Booking an operation without a residual volume, a flow study and an upper tract scan.
Forgetting the urine culture in a man with residual urine and repeated burning.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.bph.diagnosis.title: Naming the disease, grading it, and setting the threshold
skill.bph.diagnosis.oneLine: A statement with the burden, the residual, the kidneys and the referral line
skill.bph.diagnosis.why: A diagnosis of prostatic enlargement alone decides nothing: the same gland needs watching, tablets or an operation depending on the burden score, the residual urine and what the kidneys show. The diagnostic statement must carry all three, plus the line at which this patient leaves primary care.

teach.heading: The diagnostic statement
teach.body:
A complete diagnosis names the obstruction, its type and its toll: benign prostatic enlargement with chronic retention and early back-pressure change, or acute on chronic retention with infection. Add the symptom grade, the residual volume, the kidney numbers, and whether the upper tracts are dilated, since each changes the urgency.

The shared symptom score annexure grades the burden from mild through moderate to severe with its bother question; record it at the first visit and repeat it to judge every later treatment. A large symptom score with a small gland still needs treatment, and a large gland with no symptoms still needs watching.

teach.heading: Referral thresholds
teach.body:
Refer the same day for acute retention, infected retention with fever, visible blood with clots, or vomiting and drowsiness suggesting uraemia. Refer onward to urology for a hard or nodular gland, a raised or rising marker, recurrent infection, stones, or any dilatation of the upper tracts.

From a primary clinic without a scanner, the referral note should carry the story in numbers: years of symptoms, the bother score, the urine result, the kidney numbers, whether the bladder was palpable, and what the prostate felt like. A man who fails a trial without catheter, or who retains again within weeks, has declared himself surgical.

probes.q: What four facts belong in a complete BPH diagnostic statement?
probes.a: The obstruction with its retention type, the symptom grade, the residual volume with kidney numbers, and whether the upper tracts are dilated.

probes.q: A large gland with no symptoms meets a small gland with severe symptoms. Which needs treatment?
probes.a: Treatment follows the burden and the damage, not the grams: the small gland with severe symptoms needs treatment, while the large silent gland needs watching with a symptom score, urine, kidneys and residual.

probes.q: Which findings send the patient to urology rather than continued primary care?
probes.a: A hard or nodular gland, a raised or rising marker, recurrent infection, stones, dilated upper tracts, or a failed trial without catheter with early re-retention.

pitfalls: Stating prostatic enlargement without a grade, a residual or the kidney numbers.
Treating grams instead of burden: operating on size alone or ignoring severe symptoms in a small gland.
Keeping a re-retaining man in primary care after he has failed a catheter-free trial.

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.tx.bph.management.title: Managing prostatic obstruction from watch to operation
skill.tx.bph.management.oneLine: Advice and watching for the mild, tablets by class for the bothersome, operation for the failing
skill.tx.bph.management.why: Most men with mild symptoms need advice and watching, not tablets; the wrong tablet in the wrong bladder causes retention; and the right operation at the right time protects the kidneys for years. Management is a ladder, and knowing which rung the patient stands on matters more than knowing any single drug name.

teach.heading: Watchful waiting and the advice that works
teach.body:
Mild, barely bothersome symptoms with a low bother score are managed without drugs: explain the slow course, cut evening fluids, tea, coffee and alcohol, practise double voiding with unhurried bladder training, and treat constipation. Review with a repeated symptom score, urine test, kidney numbers and residual volume.

Safety-net every watched man: seek care for inability to pass urine, fever with burning, visible blood, or vomiting with swelling of the feet. Watching is active surveillance with a return plan, not discharge.

teach.heading: Drug classes and their place
teach.body:
Bothersome moderate to severe symptoms start with an alpha-blocker, which relaxes the gland muscle and bladder neck for relief within weeks; warn of dizziness on standing, falls in the elderly, ejaculatory changes, and the floppy-iris warning before any cataract operation.

An enlarged gland gains a second drug that shrinks it over months and lowers the future risk of retention and operation, and the two are combined when symptoms are marked and progression likely.

Storage symptoms that persist gain a bladder-calming drug only when the residual is small, since relaxing a poorly emptying bladder invites retention. Erection difficulty alongside urinary symptoms can be treated with a daily vessel-relaxing tablet, never combined with nitrate heart medicines. Review every new prescription in 4 to 12 weeks for benefit and side effects.

teach.heading: Retention, referral and the operation
teach.body:
Acute retention is relieved by urethral catheterisation, suprapubic if the urethra fails or is unsafe, recording the drained volume and checking kidney function and salts. Start a muscle-relaxing tablet and continue it for at least 3 days before a trial without catheter; men who pass the trial stay at higher risk and need urology follow-up with continued treatment.

The operation is indicated for retention that recurs or will not clear, back pressure with dilated upper tracts or failing kidneys, repeated infection, bladder stones, repeated visible bleeding from the gland, or symptoms uncontrolled by drugs.

Resection through the passage remains the reference operation, with laser removal, vaporisation, small-gland incision, open removal for very large glands, and newer lift and steam techniques chosen by gland size, bleeding risk and the need to preserve ejaculation.

In Indian practice, stabilise and catheterise at the primary centre, treat infection first, and refer to the district urologist with the full story; prolonged catheter time without a trial plan breeds infection and stricture. Watch for large-volume diuresis after relieving chronic retention, with fluid and salt monitoring.

probes.q: What advice and follow-up does watchful waiting involve?
probes.a: Cut evening fluids, tea, coffee and alcohol, practise double voiding with bladder training, treat constipation, and review with a repeated symptom score, urine test, kidney numbers and residual volume, with safety-net advice on retention, fever, blood and swelling.

probes.q: Why check the residual urine before adding a bladder-calming drug?
probes.a: Because relaxing the bladder when it already empties poorly can precipitate complete retention; bladder-calming drugs are avoided when the residual is large.

probes.q: Name four absolute indications for operation in BPH.
probes.a: Refractory or recurrent retention, back pressure with upper tract dilatation or failing kidneys, recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, and recurrent visible bleeding from the prostate.

pitfalls: Starting tablets for mild barely bothersome symptoms that needed only advice and watching.
Adding a bladder-calming drug without checking the residual urine first.
Leaving a catheter in for weeks with no trial plan and no referral while infection and stricture brew.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Anxious elderly man, restless, pressing his suprapubic area. Mild pallor, moist tongue, no jaundice.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 88 regular. Blood pressure 150/90. Respiratory rate 18. SpO2 96 percent on room air. Afebrile.

skill.gen.edema.finding: Mild pitting oedema over both ankles, fading by morning. No facial puffiness.

skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.finding: Both kidneys ballotable with mild tenderness at the renal angles. No gross mass felt.

skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.finding: Globular tense tender midline swelling rising midway to the navel. Cannot get below it. Dull to percussion with a convex upper border.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.finding: Normal anal tone, smooth rectal walls, no mass. No blood or mucus on the glove. Prostate assessed separately.

skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.finding: Symmetrically enlarged firm rubbery prostate with a smooth surface. Central groove preserved. Rectal lining moves freely. Non-tender. Upper border just reachable.

usg_kub.label: Ultrasound of kidneys, bladder and prostate
usg_kub.result: Prostate 45 g with median lobe projection. Bladder wall thickened with 280 mL residual urine. No upper tract dilatation. No stone.
usg_kub.note: Confirms enlargement with a significant residual and, importantly, still normal upper tracts, so relief now can prevent back-pressure damage.

urine_routine.label: Urine routine and microscopy
urine_routine.result: Acidic urine with 10 to 12 pus cells per high power field, 2 to 3 red cells, trace protein, no sugar.
urine_routine.note: Infection behind residual urine needs a culture before antibiotics; sterile pus in acid urine would instead raise tuberculosis.

renal_function.label: Blood urea and creatinine
renal_function.result: Urea 48 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, at the upper limit of normal. Sodium and potassium normal.
renal_function.note: A raised urea with creatinine at the upper limit in a retained man warns of back pressure; trend both after relief.

psa_counselled.label: Counselled serum prostate marker
psa_counselled.result: Mildly raised, in keeping with gland volume. Counselled before testing, drawn when free of infection.
psa_counselled.note: Enlargement itself raises the marker mildly; a high or rising value needs cancer evaluation, and gland-shrinking drugs halve it.

urine_culture.label: Urine culture and sensitivity
urine_culture.result: Sent before antibiotics. Growth awaited at 48 hours.
urine_culture.note: Residual urine breeds infection, so culture before treating; never let it delay catheter relief.

sugar_hba1c.label: Fasting sugar and HbA1c
sugar_hba1c.result: Fasting sugar mildly raised; HbA1c awaited.
sugar_hba1c.note: Sugar disease worsens infection and numbs the bladder, so control is part of the urinary plan.

uroflow.label: Uroflowmetry
uroflow.result: Deferred until after the trial without catheter.
uroflow.note: Flow numbers are meaningful only on a relief-assisted void; book it with the catheter-free trial.

ecg.label: Electrocardiogram
ecg.note: Not needed tonight; it joins the fitness workup only if an operation is booked.

cystoscopy.label: Cystoscopy
cystoscopy.note: Not indicated now: no visible clots, no suspected pocket or growth. Revisit if bleeding recurs or stones are suspected.

differentialModel.answer: Benign prostatic enlargement with acute on chronic urinary retention. Consider carcinoma of the prostate, urethral stricture, urinary infection with prostatitis, bladder stone, and a neurogenic bladder from sugar disease.

diagnosis.answer: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with acute on chronic urinary retention and early back-pressure change.

managementModel.answer: Relieve with urethral catheterisation and record the drained volume, correct fluids and treat the urinary infection by culture, start an alpha-blocker with a planned trial without catheter, and refer to urology for symptom grading, marker review, discussion of resection, and arranged follow-up.

teachingPoints: The tempo tells the type: three years of weak stream ending in hours of painful inability is acute on chronic retention, not a first-night problem.
A cold capsule the previous evening is the classic trigger: always ask which new medicine preceded the stoppage.
Overflow dampness for months means the bladder never emptied; the palpable dome, not the leakage story, is the diagnosis.
A smooth symmetrical gland with a preserved groove favours BPH, but terminal red urine twice still needs growth and stone excluded.
Urea 48 with creatinine at the upper limit is the kidney asking for relief; trend both after catheterisation and scan the upper tracts.
Relief comes before assessment: the prostate cannot be judged while the bladder is full, and a trial without catheter needs muscle-relaxant cover and a urology follow-up.
